common_name: Rosy Dawn Colchicum (Fragrant Late-Flowering Hybrid Autumn Crocus)

planting.note: Plant corms 4-5 inches deep and 6-9 inches apart in late summer in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Rosy Dawn is a strong, late-flowering hybrid raised by Barr and Sons that produces some of the largest blooms of any garden colchicum.

directions: Plant the corms 4 to 5 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun during late summer, spacing them 6 to 9 inches apart so the naked rosy-purple flowers have room to open in autumn before any leaves appear. Rosy Dawn was raised by the historic Barr and Sons nursery and remains one of the largest and showiest colchicum hybrids, its tessellated, goblet-shaped blooms carrying a broad white throat and golden stamens on sturdy stems that resist wind and rain better than many colchicums. Because this selection is unusually fertile, expect occasional self-sown seedlings to appear around the parent clump in following seasons. Broad, glossy dark-green leaves emerge the following spring, must be allowed to die back naturally, and all parts of the plant are toxic if ingested.

common_name: Alboplenum Colchicum (Rare Double White Autumn Crocus)

planting.note: Plant corms 4-5 inches deep in late summer in humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to very light shade; Alboplenum is a rare, slow-multiplying double white sport of the common autumn crocus and performs best when left undisturbed for years.

directions: Set the corms 4 to 5 inches deep in humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to very light shade during late summer, since this exceptionally rare double white form is slower to multiply than single-flowered autumn crocus and benefits from being left undisturbed for years. Each corm sends up multiple ruffled, fully double white blooms with no visible stamens in early autumn, the petals gradually fading to a soft blush pink as they age. First recognized with an RHS award back in the nineteenth century, Alboplenum remains a connoisseur's bulb prized for its unusual flower form rather than for vigor or rapid increase. Strap-shaped leaves follow in spring, photosynthesize through early summer, then go dormant, and the entire plant is toxic if eaten.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 2-3 inches deep in fall in gritty, sharply drained sandy soil in full sun; this Iberian and North African species needs a dry summer rest and is best grown in a raised bed, scree, or bulb frame where winter wet is controlled.

directions: Plant the small bulbs 2 to 3 inches deep in gritty, fast-draining sandy soil in full sun during fall, ideally in a raised bed, bulb frame, or alpine trough where winter wet can be controlled. Native to open coastal pine woodlands of Iberia and Morocco, this diminutive snowflake sends up three thread-like leaves alongside slender stems bearing a few small nodding white flowers flushed with pink at the base from late winter into early spring. It is considerably less cold-hardy and more drought-tolerant in summer than the familiar spring and summer snowflakes, and resents heavy, moisture-retentive ground. In regions with wet summers, grow it under glass or in a scree bed to replicate the dry dormancy it experiences in the wild.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3 inches deep in early to mid-fall in humus-rich, moisture-retentive woodland soil in partial to full shade; this Aegean island species is one of the later-flowering snowdrops and is best sited under deciduous shade that develops as it goes dormant.

directions: Plant the bulbs 3 inches deep in humus-rich, moisture-retentive woodland soil in partial to full shade during early to mid-fall, siting them where deciduous canopy will shade the ground once the plant goes dormant in early summer. This Aegean island species is immediately recognizable by its broad, dark, matte-green leaves and by the single bold green mark covering more than half of each inner petal, distinguishing it from the closely related, brighter-leaved Galanthus woronowii. It is one of the later-flowering snowdrop species, typically opening after many of the earlier nivalis forms have already faded. Left undisturbed in leaf-mold-rich soil, it slowly forms an expanding clump alongside other woodland bulbs.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3 inches deep in early fall, or move clumps 'in the green' right after flowering, into humus-rich soil in partial shade; Lady Elphinstone is a historic 1890 double-flowered cultivar with yellow rather than green inner petal markings.

directions: Plant the bulbs 3 inches deep in humus-rich soil in partial shade during early fall, or move established clumps 'in the green' right after flowering for best establishment, as with most double snowdrop selections. First discovered in Cheshire in 1890, this historic double-flowered form replaces the usual green markings on its many inner petal segments with a distinctive soft yellow, giving the nodding blooms an unusually warm glow for a snowdrop. The yellow coloring can occasionally revert to green for a season after a clump is lifted and divided, but plants typically return to their characteristic yellow markings once resettled and left undisturbed. Award-winning and slow to multiply, it is best treated as a prized specimen for a shaded rock garden or woodland edge rather than a mass planting.

common_name: Orange Glow Winter Aconite (Deep Orange-Yellow Selection)

planting.note: Plant tubers 2-3 inches deep in early fall in humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil in full sun to light shade; Orange Glow is a selection valued for flowers in a deeper orange-yellow than the species, though it naturalizes somewhat less freely.

directions: Plant the small tubers 2 to 3 inches deep in humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil in full sun to light shade in early fall, siting them where they receive good light through late winter before nearby deciduous trees leaf out. This selection produces cup-shaped flowers in a notably richer, deeper orange-yellow than the species, appearing atop a collar of finely divided green bracts in late winter to earliest spring, often pushing through the last snow. It prefers a sunnier spot than typical winter aconite and, as a result, tends to self-sow and naturalize somewhat less freely than the species form. Allow the ferny foliage to die back naturally by late spring, since the tubers rely on this brief growth period to recharge for the following winter bloom.
